- Popup lets you customize border, but you have to center the window yourself.

- https://github.com/nvim-lua/popup.nvim/pull/10

```lua
local win_id, win = popup.create(bufnr, {
    title = 'Harpoon',
    highlight = 'HarpoonWindow',
    borderhighlight = 'HarpoonBorder',
    minwidth = config.width or 60,
    minheight = config.height or 10,
    pos = 'center',
    borderchars = config.borderchars or { '─', '│', '─', '│', '╭', '╮', '╯', '╰' },
})
```

Not sure if this is the same issue but because all instances of nvim uses the same file and autosave using the in-memory copy of the file so a second nvim instance can overwrite the changes saved in the first one, causing the saved marks for all other project to revert back to their original state when the nvim first load.

To solve this we can either reload config json(`harpoon.json`) before writing or have one file for each project (will still have this problem if there are multiple nvim instances for the same project but should be less of a problem for most cases).

Reproduce:
1. (proj1) cd proj1 && nvim -u ../init.nvim file1
1. (proj2) cd proj2 && nvim -u ../init.nvim file1
1. (proj1) add mark
1. (proj1) close nvim
1. (proj1) # cd proj1 && nvim -u ../init.nvim file1 # _marks should still be there_
1. (proj2) close nvim
1. (proj1) cd proj1 && nvim -u ../init.nvim file1
1. (proj1) **marks are gone**

Adding on to the issue with multiple instances of neovim running at once, for anyone that uses tmux with a plugin like [tmux-continuum](https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tmux-continuum) or [tmux-resurrect](https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tmux-resurrect), you may run into an issue of your marks reverting back to a certain state after reboot or tmux server restart.

I had this problem, and it seems that the reason for it was because tmux-resurrect was restoring neovim processes in the background, which were also using harpoon. For that reason, there was some overlap writing to `harpoon.json` and marks were reverted back to a certain state, probably in relation to the problem @freehaha brought up.
 
I managed to solve this by adding this line to my tmux configuration:
`set -g @resurrect-processes 'false'`

That basically just disables tmux-resurrect from restoring processes like neovim when the tmux server starts. That way, no random neovim processes are started in the background and harpoon works perfectly because it's only dealing with one project at a time. Hopefully this can help someone else that is facing a similar/the same problem.

> I am worried because I see `pane = true`. should this be based on config?

That's what's happening. To configure tmux to work with windows, you specify a window index, i.e., an integer, like so:

```lua
lua require("harpoon.tmux").sendCommand(1, 'make')
```

However, if you want to this to work with a pane, you specify its position with a string, i.e.

```lua
lua require('harpoon.term').sendCommand('{bottom-right}', 'make')
```

So, we're using the type of the of the first parameter to indicate that we're going to a pane, otherwise we're specifying the window.

```lua
local subscriptions = {}
local function notify(message, f, ...)
    if type(f) == "function" then
        local ret = f(...)
        subscriptions[message] = ret
        return ret
    end
    subscriptions[message] = f
    return f
end

local function take(message)
    local ret = subscriptions[message]
    subscriptions[message] = nil
    return ret
end

local function notifier(message, f)
    return function(...)
        notify(message, f, ...)
    end
end

return {
    Subscriptions = subscriptions,
    Notify = notify,
    Take = take,
    Notifier = notifier
}
```

I did some profiling and benchmarks of my own using `plenary.profile` and `plenary.benchmark` and didn't see such huge gains, but was able to improve things.


Example benchmark code:
```
 local out = io.open("bench.log", "a")
 out:write(string.format("%s\n", 
     require('plenary.profile').benchmark(1, require("harpoon.mark").store_offset)
 ))
```




I got some odd results when benching `store_offset()` with high number of looped iterations. This could be some CPU throttling or laptop background work, idk. But it doesn't really reflect real-world use case anyway, so I went with a single iteration repeated many times.

> - Avg of 10 runs of 10 iterations of `store_offset()`:
>   - `vim.fn.json_decode`: 0.270637
>   - `vim.json.decode`: 0.349109

> - Avg of 10 runs of 100 iterations of `store_offset()`:
>   - `vim.fn.json_decode`: 1.689
>   - `vim.json.decode`: 1.74843


- Avg of 200 runs of 1 iteration of `store offset()`:
  - using `vim.fn.json_decode` before this PR: 0.226048
  - using `vim.fn.json_decode` @ 0e414fd: 0.0449416
  - using `vim.json.decode` @ 0e414fd: 0.032941
  - using `vim.json.decode` @ 61b24a7 : 0.0234444  🚀🚀🚀🚀


For that last bullet, I realized we can avoid a ton of io and JSON decodes by just getting the marks once and passing them through as a parameter to a lot of these functions. I passed the preloaded marks as an argument to several functions, and within those functions I handle the `marks == nil` case for any call sites that aren't passing them in and are still relying on the function to pull them from the config. Using this approach for `store_offset()` I was able to see a 10x performance improvement on buffer switching in testing.

@ThePrimeagen lmk if you prefer not to pass marks like this, or if prefer a bigger refactor, but IMO still readable and minimal grossness for a big perf win.

> How does grapple handle scratch buffers?

Grapple handles scratch buffers as good as it can with its data model. That is, a scratch buffer is tagged as a file with an empty `""` file path.

This could certainly be improved on with better identification when the file path is not available. In addition, any tags associated with a scratch buffer should not be persisted (grapple does not currently do this).

---

> Did you measure perf impacts of adding alot tag context and resolving logic?

Measure explicitly? No. I have run a few empirical tests with 100+ tags and no slow down was observed. I have little experience benchmarking, but would be glad to try and run a few to get a measurable baseline.

---

> How does grapple handle paths outside of the git dirs, for example relative as `../../someproject` ? Are then absolute paths used?

Absolute paths are always used. There are pros and cons to that decision. The pros are that file tags don't have to know about what scope they're in, they just exist. The cons are that if the underlying directory that the tags are saved to move, they will all become invalid. But, how often are project directories moved around?

---

> Does `global namespace` mean always valid? If so, then you should explain the precedence of resolving tag bindings or how clashes are handled otherwise.

The `global` scope is simply a [special scope](https://github.com/cbochs/grapple.nvim/blob/main/lua/grapple/scope_resolvers.lua#L11) that is given the name `__global__` where all tags would be saved to if the user chooses that scope.

I'm not entirely sure I understand your last comment here. Scopes are not (currently) _chosen_ dynamically. The scope itself will resolve dynamically (e.g. `git`), but the user will only set the scope type once during startup. There is no precedence to be had between scopes types like `global` and `git`, they exist on their own. If the user chooses `global` during plugin setup, then Grapple will only show tags that have been saved globally.

The only precedence that exists is for scope types that could fail, i.e. `git`. In this case the fallback scope is [stated](https://github.com/cbochs/grapple.nvim#project-scopes) for when the user is not in a git repo:

> `git`: tags are scoped to the current git repository, **fallback**: `static`

I hope that answered your question! Apologies if I'm misunderstanding the question.

---

> Does grapple support direct access to unordered keybindings via keybindings, ie <leader>j opening the first git tag file? I dont see anything like this in the README. Thats my main use case for harpoon.

Good question! I suppose this isn't mentioned explicitly in the docs. The API method [`grapple#cycle`](https://github.com/cbochs/grapple.nvim#grapplecycle) (you will have to expand the Usage section to access the link) will default to the first tag when invoked. So, if you don't have any files open or are in a file that is not tagged, the first tagged file would be selected.

---

> I kinda like the idea to have both global and local scoped tags into project files, but I feel like git-local tags of a project should be user-controllable read from the git repo.

Do you mean that tags should be saved to the local git repo / directory, rather than to a known save path like `vim.fn.stdpath("data") / "harpoon.json"`? That could be an interesting avenue to explore. I kind of like that :)

---

> For each git repos itself, there should be however a way to reference it and I dont understand, why harpoon has no overview of all the repos to make things like [telescope-project](https://github.com/nvim-telescope/telescope-project.nvim) superfluous.

This could be a good improvement. Some overview or good way to manage _all_ your tags across repos would be fantastic. Grapple has [some support](https://github.com/cbochs/grapple.nvim#scope-popup-menu) for this, but needs improvement since Grapple now lazily loads scopes.

Hey, I created something simple for myself using tabline framework that may be of your interest.
![Screenshot 2023-05-08 at 12 23 33](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15686693/236800511-e33bf9c7-830b-45ab-8f3a-df6bf7493970.png)

```lua
-- put this in a lua file like bufferline.lua and require in your init.lua

local function get_marks()
	local h = require("harpoon")
	local config = h.get_mark_config()
	return config.marks
end

local function normalize_path(item)
	local Path = require("plenary.path")
	return Path:new(item):make_relative(vim.loop.cwd())
end

local colors = {
	black = "#000000",
	white = "#ffffff",
	bg = "#181A1F",
	bg_sel = "#282c34",
	temp = "#287c34",
	fg = "#696969",
}

local function make_row(text, opts)
	local row = { text }
	for k, v in pairs(opts) do
		row[k] = v
	end
	return row
end

local function create_pane(f, filename, opts)
	f.set_fg(colors.fg)
	f.add({ "", fg = colors.black, bg = colors.bg_sel })
	if filename then
		f.add(make_row(f.icon(filename) .. " ", opts))
		f.add(make_row(vim.fn.fnamemodify(filename, ":t"), opts))
	end
	f.add({ "", bg = colors.bg_sel, fg = colors.black })
end

local render = function(f)
	f.add({ "  Radioactive ", fg = "#bb0000" })

	local items = get_marks()
	local found = false
	local current_file = normalize_path(vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(0))
	for _, item in ipairs(items) do
		local selected = current_file == item.filename
		if not found and selected then
			found = true
		end
		local fg = selected and f.icon_color(item.filename) or nil
		create_pane(f, item.filename, { fg = fg, bg = colors.bg_sel })
	end

	if not found then
		create_pane(f, current_file, { fg = colors.temp, bg = colors.bg_sel, gui = "italic" })
	end

	f.add_spacer()

	f.make_tabs(function(info)
		f.add({ "", fg = colors.black, bg = colors.bg_sel })
		f.add({ " " .. info.index .. " ", fg = info.current and colors.white or nil })
		f.add({ "", bg = colors.bg_sel, fg = colors.black })
	end)
end

require("tabline_framework").setup({
	render = render,
	hl = { fg = "#abb2bf", bg = "#181A1F" },
	hl_sel = { fg = "#abb2bf", bg = "#282c34" },
	hl_fill = { fg = "#ffffff", bg = "#000000" },
})

```

Here's my opinion as a minimalist ~ hopefully it's at least slightly thoughtful. My general stance is that it's better to avoid adding features unless they're somewhat widely beneficial or provide novel utility.

The predefined behavior provided by this feature makes me wonder, "what if I want to use a different message?," "what if I want to change the log level?," and so on.

I don't think the answer is to add more configuration.

If this were added then it seems like a more general approach would be to allow the user to provide a callback function that receives the buffer name as an argument so that the user can provide their own custom behavior rather calling vim.notify for them.

But, that then begs the question: why do even need to provide a callback mechanism in the first place?

Users already have to configure harpoon keybindings in their config and it's pretty easy to bind to a function that calls vim.notify before or after calling harpoon.mark.add_file() today. Thus, it doesn't seem this is core functionality that the plugin should provide given how easy it is for users to call vim.notify themselves in their own custom keybindings.

The only small roadblock is that `get_buf_name()` isn't a public function. This means that the user would need to call `require('harpoon.utils').normalize_path(vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(0))` to get the buffer name, but that's not really that hard to do either IMO.

That's more or less why I don't think this feature should be added ~ this behavior seems like it'd be better off in your init.lua rather than in harpoon. That's just my opinion, though.

Related-to: #317 

Unlike #317, this PR has one additional difference which might (or might not) tip the scales for someone -- this PR differentiates between when a buffer is added and when a buffer is not added (because it's already marked).

In my opinion this PR would also benefit from using a callback function (as described in #317) but with an additional `already_exists` boolean to differentiate the two scenarios.

I don't know if that would be reason enough to support this feature, though, so please don't waste your time updating PRs based on a random cat's opinion unless someone else chimes in. I'm just a random harpoon user.

`:h buftype`

```vim
acwrite	buffer will always be written with |BufWriteCmd|s

"acwrite" implies that the buffer name is not related to a file, like
"nofile", but it will be written.  Thus, in contrast to "nofile" and
"nowrite", ":w" does work and a modified buffer can't be abandoned
without saving.  For writing there must be matching |BufWriteCmd|,
|FileWriteCmd| or |FileAppendCmd| autocommands.
```

For those using [lazy.nvim](https://github.com/folke/lazy.nvim) plugin manager and want to utilize its lazy loading conventions by defining a `keys` object to trigger the loading of harpoon, you still totally can 🤘

Just make sure you `local harpoon` outside of your `config` func, and store to that in your `config` func, and then your `keys` will be able to access the same harpoon object 🤌

For example, in my `lua/jl/plugins/harpoon.lua`, I'm doing this...

```lua
local harpoon -- Ensure we only interact with local harpoon object 🦈

return {
  'ThePrimeagen/harpoon',
  branch = 'harpoon2', -- Temp; Will be merged soonish 🔥
  dependencies = {
    'nvim-lua/plenary.nvim',
  },
  keys = {
    { '<Leader>gh', function () harpoon.ui:toggle_quick_menu(harpoon:list()) end },
    { '<Leader>ga', function () harpoon:list():append() end },
    { '<Leader>gj', function () harpoon:list():select(1) end },
    { '<Leader>gk', function () harpoon:list():select(2) end },
    { '<Leader>gl', function () harpoon:list():select(3) end },
    { '<Leader>g;', function () harpoon:list():select(4) end },
  },
  config = function ()
    harpoon = require("harpoon"):setup() -- Notice we're storing to parent context 👆
  end,
}
```

I like the `.setup()` convention lazy.nvim expects too, but honestly this work just fine!

@ThePrimeagen I have done a little debugging and the underlying issue is caused by the `BufLeave` autocmd. Order definitely matters when it comes to autocmd trickery.

When you call `vsplit` a new split window is created with the *current* buffer (the menu buffer). When you call `nvim_set_current_buf` the `BufLeave` autocmd is executed, the menu is closed, and `nvim_buf_delete` is called *before* the new buffer is set in the window. `nvim_buf_delete` closes the windows containing deleted buffers, meaning that the window is closed before it ever contains the new buffer.

No split appears to be created, even though one was created for maybe a few milliseconds, because the splits are always closed immediately by `nvim_buf_delete`.

The options, as far as I can tell, are:

1. This fix
2. `vim.schedule_wrap` the `BufLeave` autocmd callback and call `close_menu` instead of `toggle_menu` in it to ensure the menu is only closed after `select_menu_item` is executed.

`auto-save.nvim` probably shouldn't be auto-saving non-normal buffers in the first place... imo this is something that should be addressed in that plugin. I check buftype and use `noautocmd write` in my autosave plugin to avoid this.

You should be able to prevent this behavior in your config by adding those checks to the `condition` function in your `auto-save.nvim` config. Something like this:

```lua
condition = function(buf)
  if vim.bo[buf].filetype == "harpoon" then
    return false
  end
  -- ... the rest of your condition code
end
```

You could also disable auto-save for all non-normal buffers by returning false if `buftype ~= ""` instead.

-- Function to find the root directory of the project
local function find_project_root()
    ---@type string
    local current_dir = vim.uv.cwd()
    local marker_files = { ".git", "package.json", ".sln" }

    -- Check each parent directory for the existence of a marker file or directory
    while current_dir ~= "/" do
        for _, marker in ipairs(marker_files) do
            local marker_path = current_dir .. "/" .. marker
            if vim.fn.isdirectory(marker_path) == 1 or vim.fn.filereadable(marker_path) == 1 then
                return current_dir
            end
        end
        current_dir = vim.fn.resolve(current_dir .. "/..")

                    if bufnr ~= -1 then

I have been looking into this a bit and there are at least two issues going on here.
1. The display name does not match the name of the file so the current `BufLeave` function does not always update the position. I have recreated this with a unit test and have a fix for this case.
2. `VimLeavePre` is called, but in `_for_each_list()` seen is not true and lists is sometimes nil.

- `self.data.seen` is nil or empty
- `self.lists` is nil or empty

Ok, I've been mulling over this for a few days, I think any solution that maintains the current paradigms requires either:
- Making `append`/`prepend` async and taking a callback (or returning a promise/future)
- Having an additional async version of existing functions like `create_list_item_async`, `append_async`, and `prepend_async` then dealing with when each errors, or what version of `create_list_item` they call. 

Both those don't sound very good to me (happy to provide more details on the designs I considered here if that is helpful).

I am starting to think that the current coupling between `append` and `create_list_item` is likely the issue here. It seems like `append`/`prepend` are trying to do two different tasks:
1. Add a pre-constructed item to the list: `append(something)`
1. Construct a new item and append it to the list: `apend(nil)`

Pretty sure the first has no reason to ever be async, but the second does (see original post above).

Separating the intent of appending an item from that of creating a new one should help make an API that is more flexible/composable, still feels good, and supports async item creation while keeping `append` non-async.

This would require a breaking change where `append(nil)` is no longer considered valid. And if we want to avoid having two versions of "create item", then the one version we do have will have to be async (via either callback or promise).

`append(nil)` might become something like `create_new_item(nil, function(item) append(item) end)` (or a future/promise variant).

Hopefully there's an even better solution, and maybe the path forward is to just say that async item creation is not supported by the harpoon API and requires external functions. But if we do want to support async item creation in the harpoon api, I am having trouble seeing how to do it without a breaking change

If you want an item that you add when in one cwd to show up in the list when you are in another cwd, then you need to change your key to something other than `vim.loop.cwd()`. Then you could change the create_list_item to something like this:
```lua
            create_list_item = function(_, item)
                if item == nil then
                    item = vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(
                        vim.api.nvim_get_current_buf()
                    )
                end

                if type(item) == "string" then
                    local name = require("plenary.path"):new(item):absolute()
                    local bufnr = vim.fn.bufnr(name, false)

                    local pos = { 1, 0 }
                    if bufnr ~= -1 then
                        pos = vim.api.nvim_win_get_cursor(0)
                    end
                    item = {
                        value = name,
                        context = {
                            row = pos[1],
                            col = pos[2],
                        },
                    }
                end
                return item
            end,
```

Okay, I think I have a better solution now. Instead of the `ignoreBuffers` approach, [`vim.bo.buftype`](https://neovim.io/doc/user/options.html#'buftype') can be checked before append or prepend. According to the docs the `buftype` will be empty for a normal buffer. Buffers like NvimTree have a type of `nowrite` and the Harpoon jumplist has a type of `acwrite`. Only adding empty `buftype` buffers to the jumplist should fix this problem. I'll start working on a PR to implement this.

Huh. Apparently `<C-m>` is bound to `<CR>` internally in Neovim and Vim. So hitting either produces the same result. As you have `<C-m>` bound to `toggle_quick_menu`, that must be causing `<CR>` to open up the same.
from `:h key-notation`:
```
notation	meaning		    equivalent	decimal value(s)	 
-----------------------------------------------------------------------  
<Nul>		zero			CTRL-@	  0 (stored as 10) *<Nul>*
<BS>		backspace		CTRL-H	  8	*backspace*
<Tab>		tab			CTRL-I	  9	*tab* *Tab*
							*linefeed*
<NL>		linefeed		CTRL-J	 10 (used for <Nul>)
<CR>		carriage return		CTRL-M	 13	*carriage-return* <-------- This one here
<Return>	same as <CR>				*<Return>*
```

So just don't map the `<C-m>` key in vim or neovim. It internally treats it as `<CR>`. And as for allowing the user to remap the keys, there is nothing stopping you from remapping the key after Harpoon is set up. Just like you delete the key binding.

### Harpoon Setup
```
		local harpoon = require("harpoon")
		local truncateAt = require('config.harpoon-truncate')
		local Path = require("plenary.path")
		local function normalize_path(buf_name, root)
			return Path:new(buf_name):make_relative(root)
		end
		harpoon:setup({
			default = {
				create_list_item = function(config, name)
					name = name
						or normalize_path(
							vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(
								vim.api.nvim_get_current_buf()
							),
							config.get_root_dir()
						)

					local bufnr = vim.fn.bufnr(name, false)

					local fileDirectory = vim.fn.expand('%:p:h:t')
					local fileName = vim.fn.expand('%:t')
					local pathname = fileDirectory .. '/' .. fileName
					local newName = name;
					if (string.len(name) >= truncateAt.trucateLength(name)) then
						newName = Path:new(name):shorten(2)
						-- or
						-- newName = pathname
					end

					local pos = { 1, 0 }
					if bufnr ~= -1 then
						pos = vim.api.nvim_win_get_cursor(0)
					end

					return {
						value = name,
						context = {
							row = pos[1],
							col = pos[2],
							name = newName
						},
					}
				end,
				display = function(list_item)
					return list_item.context.name
				end,

			}
		})
```

### Truncate file
```
local HarpoonText = {}

function HarpoonText:trucateLength()
	local win = vim.api.nvim_list_uis()

	local ui_fallback_width = 69;
	local ui_width_ratio = 0.62569;
	local width = ui_fallback_width

	if #win > 0 then
		-- no ackshual reason for 0.62569, just looks complicated, and i want
		-- to make my boss think i am smart
		width = math.floor(win[1].width * ui_width_ratio)
	end

	local truncateAt = math.floor((vim.o.columns - width) / 2) - 1

	return truncateAt
end

return HarpoonText

```

@gvolpe Yes, I noticed this bug, I got it working by using a indexOf helper function to get the index of the mark in the list correctly. Here it is if you want, and I will include it in this PR
```lua
local function list_indexOf(list, predicate)
    for i, v in ipairs(list) do
        if predicate(v) then
            return i
        end
    end
    return -1
end
```

I've been using my "fixed" version of `remove_at` for the last couple days; in order to make Telescope play nice with it, we need a way to represent the `nil` values in between the populated indexes of the `list` (since the list only collapses back to its "compact" length once there are no "holes" in between items, in order to preserve the list indexes); something like this:

```lua
-- excerpt from my neovim config

local harpoon_get_paths = function(files)
  local paths = {}
  local items = files.items
  local len = files._length

  for i = 1, len do
    paths[i] = ''
    local item = items[i]
    if item ~= nil then
      paths[i] = item.value
    end
  end

  return paths
end
```

If the problem is related to `Harpoon 2`, the problem is that when you select an item from `HarpoonList`  through the `<CR>` keybind while in the Harpoon toggle ui, it only will select the desired item but will not update the the value of `HarpoonList._index` as done by the `HarpoonList:next()` and also `HarpoonList:prev()` see the source code below:

```lua
function HarpoonList:select(index, options)
    local item = self.items[index]
    if item or self.config.select_with_nil then
        Extensions.extensions:emit(
            Extensions.event_names.SELECT,
            { list = self, item = item, idx = index }
        )
        self.config.select(item, self, options)
    end
end

---
--- @param opts? HarpoonNavOptions
function HarpoonList:next(opts)
    opts = opts or {}

    self._index = self._index + 1
    if self._index > self._length then
        if opts.ui_nav_wrap then
            self._index = 1
        else
            self._index = self._length
        end
    end

    self:select(self._index)
end

---
--- @param opts? HarpoonNavOptions
function HarpoonList:prev(opts)
    opts = opts or {}

    self._index = self._index - 1
    if self._index < 1 then
        if opts.ui_nav_wrap then
            self._index = #self.items
        else
            self._index = 1
        end
    end

    self:select(self._index)
end
```

So imho the behaviour of `HarpoonList:select()` should also update the index, so the it does not break the navigation flow and also make it consistent between all 3 methods.

map("i", "<C-m>", function()
	local state = require("telescope.actions.state")
	local selected_entry = state.get_selected_entry()
	if selected_entry.index - 1 < 1 then
		return
	end

	local curr_item = table.remove(harpoon_files.items, selected_entry.index)
	local prev_item = table.remove(harpoon_files.items, selected_entry.index - 1)

	table.insert(harpoon_files.items, selected_entry.index - 1, curr_item)
	table.insert(harpoon_files.items, selected_entry.index, prev_item)

	state.get_current_picker(prompt_bufnr):refresh(finder())
end)

```
return {

  branch = "harpoon2",
  dependencies = { "nvim-lua/plenary.nvim" },
  config = function()
    local harpoon = require("harpoon")
    harpoon:setup({
      settings = {
        save_on_toggle = true,
        save_on_change = true,
      },
    })

    -- When the Harpoon quick menu is open, press 1–9 to open that index, 0 => 10
    vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("FileType", {
      pattern = "harpoon",
      callback = function(ev)
        local map = function(lhs, idx)
          vim.keymap.set("n", lhs, function()
            harpoon:list():select(idx)
          end, { buffer = ev.buf, silent = true, nowait = true })
        end
        for i = 1, 9 do
          map(tostring(i), i)
        end
        map("0", 10)
      end,
    })

    -- Put current buffer into a specific slot (index) in the default list
    local function harpoon_set_slot(idx)
      local list = harpoon:list()
      local path = vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(0)
      if path == nil or path == "" then
        return
      end
      local item = list.config.create_list_item(list.config, path)
      for i, v in ipairs(list.items) do
        if v and v.value == item.value and i ~= idx then
          list.items[i] = nil
        end
      end
      list.items[idx] = item
    end

    -- Keymaps to set Harpoon slots 1..10
    for i = 1, 9 do
      vim.keymap.set("n", "<leader>h" .. i, function()
        harpoon_set_slot(i)
      end, { desc = "Harpoon: set slot " .. i })
    end
  end,
}
